aiExplanation: This function decides whether the array can be made **uniform**, meaning every element could end up with the same parity (all even or all odd). In a first pass it counts how many numbers are odd and how many are even, using the bitwise trick `num & 1` to test parity, while also remembering the two smallest odd values seen (`lowestOdd1` and `lowestOdd2`). The key idea is that subtracting a *smaller odd number* from an element flips that element's parity, so in a second pass any number strictly greater than one of those smallest odds is treated as convertible: an odd number gets added to the `even` tally and an even number to the `odd` tally. If either tally reaches `n`, every element is (or can be turned) even, or every element is (or can be turned) odd, so the function returns `true`; otherwise it returns `false`.

aiExplanation: This is a streamlined take on the same problem: can the array be made **uniform**, with every element sharing the same parity (all even or all odd)? The first loop counts the `odd` and `even` numbers, checking parity with the bitwise test `num & 1`, and tracks only the single smallest odd value, `lowestOdd`. Since subtracting a smaller odd number flips an element's parity, the second loop treats every number strictly greater than `lowestOdd` as convertible to the opposite parity — odd numbers are added to the `even` count and even numbers to the `odd` count. The function returns `true` when either count reaches the array length `n`, meaning all elements are (or can be made) even, or all are (or can be made) odd.
